Elections are scheduled to be held in the United States, in large part, on November 3, 2026. In these midterm elections, scheduled to occur during the second term of Republican president Donald Trump, all 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the U.S. Senate will be contested to determine the 120th United States Congress. Thirty-nine state and territorial U.S. gubernatorial elections, attorney general elections, and numerous state and local elections will also be contested.

The lead-up to the elections was marked by an inflation surge amidst the United States affordability crisis, affecting prices of gas, healthcare, and food, with the executive branch raising federal revenue by imposing the largest tax hikes in American history through tariffs. Other shared concerns cited by voters include a perception of corruption and self-dealing; democratic backsliding; mass surveillance; and foreign policy, including the 2026 Iran war, declining relations with American allies, a proposed rapprochement with Russia, coerced expansionism, and an escalating rift with the Vatican. The Trump administration politically aligned with Silicon Valley and encouraged the development of artificial superintelligence through the construction of AI data centers, and there has been a public backlash to the potential prospect of widespread unemployment as a result of AGI, its environmental impacts, and the existential risk it may pose to humanity. The administration campaigned on changing the English language to align with Trump's nationalist ideology, including the names of Lake Ontario ("Lake America") and the Gulf of Mexico ("Gulf of America"), while Democrats labeled the changes a distraction from important issues.

Trump called on Republican-led states to enact rare mid-decade redistricting to boost the party's chances of holding power ahead of expected historical losses for the incumbent party during midterm elections, which prompted reciprocal redistricting. In April 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that some parts of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 are unconstitutional. The Trump administration has used millions of taxpayer dollars to fund Republican campaign advertisements, and federal agents are going to residents' homes to question them about their citizenship and voting history.

Background

See also: Second presidency of Donald Trump § Historical evaluations and public opinion

In the 2024 United States presidential election, Republican nominee Donald Trump defeated Democratic nominee Kamala Harris. Key issues shaping the campaign included public concern for the post-pandemic recovery and rising inflation.[2][3]

ABC News, CBS News, Fox News, NBC News, the Associated Press, MS Now and CNN will use the Voter Poll by SSRS to gather voter preferences and opinions for the 2026 elections. From 2018 to 2024, ABC, NBC, CBS and CNN used data from the National Election Pool while the Associated Press and Fox News relied on AP VoteCast.[4][5]

The Republican Party performed worse than expected in the November 2025 general elections. Democratic candidates Abigail Spanberger of Virginia and Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey won their gubernatorial races over their Republican opponents by larger than expected margins. Democrats performed strongly in the concurrent state legislative elections, winning a supermajority in the New Jersey General Assembly and expanding their majority in the Virginia House of Delegates. In New York City, Democrat Zohran Mamdani, a self-identified democratic socialist, was elected mayor in a three-way race against Republican Curtis Sliwa and independent former governor Andrew Cuomo, who ran as a moderate relative to Mamdani.[6] The main theme of the elections was the United States affordability crisis.[7]

2026 election developments and analysis

Voters' views of Trump's presidency will likely be an important factor in the election.[8] During the 2025 off-year elections, exit polls found that many voted in opposition to Trump or said that he was not a factor.[9] Surveys released in late 2025 and early 2026 found that many viewed Trump's handling of the economy and immigration, two issues that propelled him to victory in the 2024 election,[10][11] negatively.[12][13] During elections held in his first term, Trump was on the minds of many who voted.[14][15][16] In September 2026, Trump featured in a two-day midterm convention in Dallas to rally support and raise funds—historically, this type of event is reserved for presidential election years, although the Democratic National Committee had previously held midterm-year party conferences in 1974, 1978 and 1982. Many Republicans on the ballot attended, but many also chose to forego the event, which RNC Chairman Joe Gruters dubbed a "Trump-a-Palooza."[17][18][19]

The outbreak of the 2026 Iran war on February 28 introduced further complications, with rising gasoline prices and other economic challenges emerging as central electoral concerns.[20][21] Analysts argued that gasoline prices represented the most direct channel through which the costs of the Iran war were transmitted to American voters, and that domestic electoral pressure from fuel costs was a primary political driver behind the Trump administration's push toward a ceasefire ahead of the November midterms.[22] Polling released by CNN in the September of 2026 showed that only 26% of voters approved of the Trump administrations handling of Iran.[23]In response to the general unpopularity and economic concerns of the Iran war, several Republican candidates have distanced themselves from Trump and his approach to the war and have called for operations in Iran to end.[24][25] Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer compared the political environment in 2026 to the one in 2006,[26] when dissatisfaction with George W. Bush's handling of the Iraq war led to many Democratic victories in the elections that year.[27] Democratic candidates have leveraged the unpopularity of the war as a campaign point.

Thus, the nearly seven-month-old war in Iran became a political liability for some vulnerable Republican candidates ahead of the November midterms. In September 2026, two Republicans in tight Senate races — Mike Rogers of Michigan and Ashley Hinson of Iowa — called for a swift end to the conflict, distancing themselves from President Trump. Hinson, who had voted six times against measures to curb Trump's war powers, said Iowans "shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran." Rogers, who had previously backed Trump's strikes, released a campaign ad urging that the war "end and end quickly." The shift came as Trump's approval rating fell to 32%, a career low, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll, with Americans souring on both his handling of the economy and the war. Diesel prices reached record highs, a particular concern in Iowa, where agriculture plays an outsized role in the state's economy. Other Republicans also moved to distance themselves: Iowa Representatives Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks reversed their stances and voted to limit Trump's war powers, while Representative Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida warned that Trump's immigration crackdown had gone too far. Democrats characterized the moves as election-year repositioning.[28] By mid-October, the same polling series put Trump's approval at 31% — a record low for either of his terms and a point below where it stood two weeks earlier. The same Reuters/Ipsos survey had Democrats ahead of Republicans 47% to 35% on the generic congressional ballot, a 12-point gap that was the widest of the election cycle.[29]

The administration's immigration policies, including deportations by ICE due to strengthened funding via the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, were also scrutinized.[30][31] Polling found that Hispanics, who were considered a key reason for Trump's victory in the 2024 election, overwhelmingly disapproved of Trump and had largely swung back towards Democrats due to economic concerns and dissatisfaction of Trump's handling of immigration and deportation.[32][33][34] An October Reuters/Ipsos poll found that majorities said the cost of living was their top issue for the election and that 76% of Americans blamed Trump's policies for increasing inflation, including 57% of Republicans.[35] Signs of an enthusiasm gap between Republican and Democratic voters were noted by analysts as possibly forecasting a Democratic "blue wave". In September 2026, American political analyst Charlie Cook described this phenomenon as a "red undertow", arguing that anticipated Democratic victories would come not from a rising Democratic tide, but a drowning Trump brand.[36]

A month before the election, polling consistently found that Democratic candidates were leading key races for state governorships and those that would determine control of the Senate, with large swings towards Democratic candidates by independent voters.[37] The New York Times highlighted how Kansas, a state that had not elected a Democratic Senator since the Second World War, had become a competitive battleground amid an unexpected surge of Democratic support deep in Republican territory.[38][39] Furthermore, a poll commissioned by The Washington Post and George Mason University had to deal with the unusual issue of far fewer Republicans (12%) willing to respond than Democrats (32%), an exceptional gap.[40][41] Democratic support came amidst multiple polls finding record-low approval ratings for Trump which some analysts considered was negatively impacting down-ballot races.[42][43][44] Trump repeatedly told voters to pretend he was on the ballot to increase Republican enthusiasm which Democrats and some analysts considered a mistake owing to his low approval ratings.[45][46][47] Increasing concerns about the Republicans' position in the November midterm elections have exposed tensions within Donald Trump's political structure. According to Reuters, Trump criticized his advisers for their election strategy, including decisions related to campaign spending and candidate selection. This is despite polls suggesting that Democrats could gain control of the House of Representatives.[48]

In October, the Trump administration called for Ukraine to replace Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the nation's president and struck a deal with Russia to purchase the country's fuel in an effort to bring down diesel prices before the elections, and deepened Russian-American cooperation. The fuel deal was criticized by Democrats and some Republicans for undercutting the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which allowed the president to waive tariffs or sanctions if he certified to Congress that doing so was in the national interest of the United States, a provision that some Democratic lawmakers concerned about Trump unilaterally lifting the sanctions against Russia pointed to in their opposition to the bill.[49]

Julian E. Zelizer has drawn a comparison between the 1966 and 2026 midterm elections. Writing for Foreign Policy in October 2026, he noted that the Republican campaign of 1966 focused on the economic cost of the Vietnam War, including growing federal deficits and inflation. He argued that the economic impact of the war in Iran, which had driven consumer prices up, gave Democrats an opening similar to the one Republicans had seized in 1966. Zelizer acknowledged that the Iran war had not reached the scale of Vietnam and likely never would, but said its economic effects had nonetheless been considerable—and in some respects clearer—and that the war had been unpopular from the outset.[50]

Political analyst Natalie Jackson told Al Jazeera that the polling pointed to a "pretty favourable" environment for Democrats. She traced this to public frustration with Trump and the economy — high costs driven in part by tariffs and the war in Iran — and said the prevailing mood was that Republicans had failed to deliver over the past two years.[51]

Foreign interference

See also: Foreign interference in the 2024 United States elections

Foreign nations have sought to interfere with the 2026 elections. Since 2016, "the Kremlin has initiated online influence operations in every American federal election cycle" according to declassified intelligence documents. According to US intelligence officials, in 2026, Russia is targeting Americans with covert online disinformation campaigns to undermine confidence in the election and seed and promote domestic divisions with the goal to "inject chaos". No evidence exists that Russia has attempted to take aim at voting machinery or compromise the voting process. US intelligence officials have described the effort as less extensive and coordinated than prior years, with officials speculating Russia is less interested in midterm races than presidential contests and is distracted by the Russo-Ukrainian war.[52]

US intelligence has speculated Iran may have engaged in online influence efforts, and in August 2026 Meta Platforms reported a small number of accounts on Facebook and Instagram originating from Iran spreading AI generated content with "anti-Republican views". US intelligence speculates that unlike prior years where China supported or opposed individual candidates based on their views, it may stay out of the 2026 elections due to fears of blowback.[52] On October 14, 2026, the social network X suspended more than 13,000 accounts linked to Iran, Russia, and China ahead of the US midterm elections.[53]

In a prime time address on July 16, Trump alleged (among other things)[54] that China had collected 220 million American voter identification files including private information in 2022 and that it amounted to election interference. Trump then declassified intelligence records he presented as evidence the US election system falls "catastrophically short". Election experts pushed back on some of the claims, stating that voter registration files are public and easily accessible in most states and would not necessarily allow interference with the voting process.[55] On September 28, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the Department of Defense would launch an effort dedicated to combating foreign meddling in US elections that would use "advanced intelligence and cyber capabilities to identify, disrupt, and neutralize foreign interference".[56] Democratic leaders of the House and Senate intelligence committees have expressed worry that Trump will use claims of foreign interference in an attempt to intervene in the midterm elections.[57]

An analysis of political advertising related to the Iran war found that 61 of the 65 ads examined between September 1 and October 14, 2026, focused on the cost of living. The ads aired more than 43,000 times on television, with an estimated total expenditure of $42 million.[58][59]

AIPAC (Pro-Israel lobby)

Less than five years after entering U.S. political campaigns, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) has raised $233 million, making it one of the best-funded groups in midterm elections. However, it has also become polarizing, with many candidates rejecting its support, and some highlighting opposition to AIPAC as a point of pride. AIPAC faces criticism and calls itself part of a bigger struggle to protect Israel. Despite challenges and shifting public opinion, AIPAC plans to continue spending heavily on campaigns.[60] The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) has invested over $54 million in U.S. congressional races through its super PAC, the United Democracy Project (UDP), making it the largest outside spender in the current election cycle. This spending reflects AIPAC's strong influence in Washington. Despite some victories, AIPAC has faced significant setbacks, such as in Michigan, where its funding failed to secure a win for its favored candidate. Critics argue that AIPAC's influence is waning, as many voters, especially Democrats, believe the U.S. is too supportive of Israel. This shift in public opinion has led to discomfort among Republicans as well. AIPAC's financial power remains strong, contributing $30 million to UDP, but its brand is becoming less favorable among candidates and voters across the political spectrum. Many candidates prefer not to mention AIPAC or its funding in their campaigns, recognizing its potential negative impact.[61] During this midterms cycle, AIPAC’s strategy appears to be shifting due to negative voter perception linked to Israel's actions in Gaza and U.S. military aid. AIPAC is now focusing on funding other groups and uniting donors rather than directly endorsing candidates.[62][63] Political analyst Trita Parsi noted AIPAC's previous power is fading, as its name is now viewed negatively. AIPAC is also planning to invest heavily in Republican candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan, trying to defeat critic Abdul El-Sayed.[64]

Attempted election subversion by Republicans

Further information: Republican Party efforts to disrupt voting after the 2024 United States presidential election, Election denial movement in the United States, and Targeting of political opponents and civil society under the second Trump administration
This section is an excerpt from Election law and voting rights under the second Trump administration.[edit]

The second Trump administration has issued executive orders and other presidential directives instituting federal department and agency actions that have impacted election administration by state governments, federal election security and campaign finance agencies, and offices within the U.S. Justice Department for enforcing voting rights protections. The administration's actions on election law and voting rights have occurred alongside the administration's targeting of political opponents and Republican Party efforts to disrupt voting after the 2024 presidential election. Election lawyers at the Brennan Center for Justice and Democracy Docket have described the administration's actions as election subversion,[65][66][67] while surveys of U.S. political scientists conducted after Trump returned to office have found a consensus that the United States is transitioning towards illiberal democracy and competitive authoritarianism.[68][69]

In January 2026, The Washington Post reported that the second Trump administration had undertaken several tactics, including mid-decade redrawing of congressional districts for partisan gain, prosecution of political opponents, and a push to change voting methods and rules, that were meant to undermine confidence in the midterm elections.[70] In October 2026, a New York Times analysis found Trump had attacked the integrity of US elections more than 70% of the days since he returned to office,[71] particularly with false claims about "rigged" voting machines and fraudulent mail-in ballots.[72][73]

Upon returning to office, the Trump administration has dismantled election security efforts across the federal government. Such cuts have included: firing or reassigning personnel at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency focused on elections; defunding training programs for the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center; eliminating the FBI's foreign influence taskforce; downsizing and announcing closure of the Foreign Malign Influence Center; and firing all members of the independent Election Assistance Commission.[74][75][76]

Trump appointed prominent 2020 election deniers into positions in government that could oversee the voting process.[77] In the lead up to the election, pro-Trump conspiracy theorists and election deniers have won local races responsible for overseeing election results,[78] and several election deniers are running for electoral offices in battleground states.[79]

SAVE America Act

This section is an excerpt from Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act.[edit]

The Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, also known as the SAVE Act or SAVE America Act, is a proposed United States federal law that requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship in order to register to vote in U.S. federal elections. The bill was introduced amid unsubstantiated claims that there was significant election fraud in previous elections, including voting by undocumented immigrants, as part of the immigration policies of the second Donald Trump administration. Opponents have claimed that the bill would disenfranchise eligible voters.

In March, the House of Representatives passed the SAVE America Act, an amended version of the previously proposed Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act. The bill, if approved by the Senate and signed into law by Trump, would have required voters to provide proof of citizenship in order to obtain or renew their voter registration. Voting rights experts said that such provisions would disenfranchise married women, racial minorities, low-income groups, and people who legally changed their name, among others.[80][81][82] The bill ultimately died in the Senate that June, with four Republicans joining Democrats to block its inclusion.[83][84]

Cancellation and nationalization of elections

In January, Trump floated the idea of illegally canceling the elections, citing an expected loss in the elections and a distrust in democratic systems.[85] White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt later stated that Trump was "speaking facetiously", and was "simply joking".[86] In February, Trump stated that the elections should be nationalized to prevent voter fraud.[87]

On February 27, The Washington Post reported that several right-wing activists are working with the Trump administration to draft an executive order which, if signed, would effectively instate a national emergency and give Trump extended powers over the elections. Trump denied the existence of such an order.[88]

According to ABC News, Trump met prominent election denier Tina Peters on October 5 at the White House. Speaking to conservative podcaster Joe Oltmann on October 8, Peters' attorney stated that Trump "is not going to relinquish control again" if he believes the elections are rigged, and that "It's better if we're going to have a civil war of any sort that it be martial law with our side in control of the armaments."[89]

Concerns over ICE at polling places

In February, Steve Bannon said the federal government was planning to send ICE to patrol polling stations in an attempt to prevent a Democratic victory, vowing to "never again allow an election to be stolen".[90] In March, Stateline reported that legislation to "restrict immigration enforcement or the presence of federal forces" near polling places and other election sites has been offered or announced in California, Connecticut, New Mexico, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Virginia and Washington.[91] The same month, the Associated Press reported that several Democratic-led states including New Mexico and Virginia are taking steps to counter potential tactics to intimidate voters.[92] In May, Ned Lamont, the governor of Connecticut, signed into law a bill that restricts immigration enforcement at locations including schools and places of worship. The legislation also prohibits law enforcement from wearing facial coverings or personal disguises.[93][94] Some federal law prohibits armed federal agents from being deployed near election sites.[95]

Federal investigations and false claims of voter fraud

Main article: Election denial movement in the United States

Internal documents reviewed by The New York Times found a widespread effort by the federal government to promote mistrust in the integrity of the 2026 election, with homeland security officials investigating over 150 nonprofit organizations they allege are helping noncitizens to vote.[96] Trump and Republicans have repeatedly made false and unsubstantiated claims of massive voter fraud by noncitizens,[97][98] with The Times describing Trump as making the case that "any Democratic election victory is suspicious on its face".[99]

As part of investigations into election-integrity, the Justice Department has demanded voter registration data from states, suing 23 states and the District of Columbia that declined to provide unredacted voter rolls; all of the sued states were led by Democrats or had been won by Joe Biden in 2020.[100] In January 2026, a federal judge blocked the Trump administration from threatening to withhold election funding from states that did not provide their voter information or alter their voter registration forms or voter systems.[101] Also in January 2026, U.S. District Judge David Carter dismissed the department's lawsuit against California, which had sought personal information including partial Social Security numbers for roughly 23 million registered voters, ruling that the demands violated privacy laws and writing that federal centralization of the data would have a "chilling effect" on voter registration; a federal judge dismissed a similar lawsuit against Oregon later that month.[102][100] The department appealed the California ruling to the Ninth Circuit. In June 2026, federal prosecutors in Los Angeles publicly accused the state of blocking a voter roll audit and said they were conducting election fraud investigations while ballots from the state's June primary were still being counted.[103]

The Department of Homeland Security engaged in a widespread effort to investigate supposed voter fraud. Per internal documents released by the advocacy group Democracy Forward, efforts have relied on the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) division of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which CNN described as part of a "phased national initiative involving voter-roll acquisition, data analysis, investigative leads and field investigations". A June 1 HSI report documented the Justice Department had reviewed more than 50.6 million records and an additional 48.4 million records from Heather Honey obtained through "independent sources of information". The 50.6 million records were speculated to have been received by unredacted voter lists handed over by over a dozen Republican states in the months prior. By October 2026, the Justice Department had sued 30 states to hand over their voter information.[104]

In July, Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin alleged they had discovered 270,000 noncitizens on voter roles in Nevada, California, New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Letters sent to states days later acknowledged the numbers had been inflated, noting Trump had stated "there may be as many as", and the letters did not offer any proof of the claims. Mullin later claimed there were 15,903 noncitizen voters in Nevada, although the Department of Homeland Security later admitted in a meeting with Nevada election officials the claim was unsubstantiated. DHS then stated 185 of the 15,903 were noncitizens of which Nevada disputed, saying after a state review all 185 were citizens and that DHS had "never provided Nevada with a list of 15,903 individuals" to begin with.[105]

Ahead of the elections, Trump made false claims of voter fraud through mail-in ballots, calling it "corrupt" and "cheating", and encouraged Republican lawmakers to pass strict voter ID laws claiming it would "guarantee the midterms" for the GOP.[106] In March 2026, Trump signed a new executive order on elections which would require the government to compile a list of eligible voters in each state and only allow the United States Post Office to send ballots to verified voters. Election experts described the effort as likely unconstitutional, and the announcement was met with promises to sue by voter rights groups and Democratic officials.[107] On September 4, Judge Indira Talwani issued a preliminary injunction against the USPS plan, finding it likely illegal and noting USPS had no authority to control mail-in voting, and Judge Carl J. Nichols issued another preliminary injunction against the plan on September 13.[108] On September 14, the Supreme Court ruled against the Trump administration's attempt to screen mail-in ballots finding the government was "unlikely to succeed on the merits" and that it would implement chaos and confusion ahead of the elections.[109] Following the ruling, state election officials were described as moving to restore faith in mail-in voting,[110] and Trump later encouraged Republicans to vote by mail.[111]

In September, the Supreme Court allowed the administration to use the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements system to check voter rolls for noncitizens, although federal law prohibits "systematically" removing voters from voter rolls 90 days before an election. The Trump administration had overhauled the system to combine social security and other data to create a master database of citizens per Executive Order 14248. Lawsuits and court rulings had previously blocked implementation of the system, with judges finding the overhaul had violated law in combining private information and had removed eligible voters from voter rolls.[112] Also in September, Homeland Security Investigations agents began going to homes in several states to ask residents about their citizenship and whether they had registered or voted. Some of the agents were armed.[113] On October 15, the Justice Department sued California and Los Angeles County, asking a court to block the counting of mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters that DHS had flagged as likely noncitizens.[114] NBC News reported on October 21 that the department was considering similar suits against other states.[115]

In October, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the Democratic Governors Association, the Nevada Democratic Party as well as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries sued the Trump administration alleging that government's pressure campaign to remove voters from state voter rolls is unlawfully interfering with the midterm elections.[116] On October 22, 2026, Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the Northern District of California issued preliminary injunction that bars the Department of Homeland Security from conducting election-related field operations in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington, and Wisconsin until the polls close on Election Day (November 3, 2026).[117][118] This injunction covers field interviews and stops being carried out by agents of the Department of Homeland Security; Martínez-Olguín stated that the scope of these operations raised voter intimidation concerns.[119]

On October 26, 2026, President Donald Trump announced a $1 million reward for information on voter fraud in past elections or the 2026 midterms, to be paid if the tip led to an arrest and conviction. Trump posted the offer on Truth Social roughly a week before the midterm elections. The offer came after the Trump administration had spent months demanding voter-registration records from state governments. The administration argued that stricter election oversight was needed to preserve public confidence in the vote. Political analysts and election officials—among them Democrats and several Republicans—characterized the administration's actions as overstepping federal authority. Several election officials told Reuters they were making preparations in case the federal government intervened in the midterms.[120]

On October 29, 2026, days before the election, the Justice Department sent letters to election officials in all 50 states reminding them of the federal requirement to preserve election record for 22 months and stating that willful violations are punishable by up to a year in prison and 1,000.[121][122] The letters, signed by Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, did not cite a specific violation or investigation.[123] A justice department spokesperson said the letter reminded states of their preservation obligations.[124] Justin Levitte, a former justice department official, said the letter looked "meant to intitmidate rather than to infom," while election law professor Joshua Douglas said he had never seen the department send such a letter nationwide days before an election.[125]

Activists say they are preparing large-scale demonstrations if the Trump administration attempts to interfere with voting or the counting of ballots. At the same time, legal experts are publishing guidance for judges on how to respond if the government attempts to take control of ballots.[126]

The war with Iran became a subject of Democratic campaigning ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. On October 24, former president Barack Obama criticized Trump's decision to launch the war during a rally in Cleveland supporting Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown and gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton. Obama described the conflict as unnecessary and criticized the administration's foreign policy, urging voters to use the midterm elections to challenge the direction of the Trump administration.[127]

FBI raids

In January 2026, FBI agents executed a search warrant at the Fulton County, Georgia, election center, seizing approximately 600 boxes of ballots and other records from the 2020 presidential election, an action election law experts described as unprecedented federal intervention in locally administered elections.[128][129] Federal investigations of the 2020 election subsequently expanded to several states: the Office of the Director of National Intelligence procured voting machines in Puerto Rico for examination in February, federal officials subpoenaed records of the partisan review of Maricopa County, Arizona's 2020 results in March, the Justice Department demanded ballots cast in Wayne County, Michigan, in April, and FBI agents questioned former poll workers in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, in May.[129]

David Becker, executive director of The Center for Election Innovation & Research, said the investigations were "about the 2026 and 2028 elections" rather than 2020, characterizing them as intimidation of election officials. John Keller, former acting head of the Justice Department's Public Integrity Section, said the administration appeared to be normalizing federal investigation of state elections in preparation for potentially challenging future results.[129]

In June 2026, FBI agents searched the Cleveland offices of the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a voter registration and community organizing group, seizing computers and questioning staff and volunteers across Ohio as part of a Justice Department investigation into the group's voter registration efforts; the Brennan Center for Justice said the search fit a pattern of federal inquiries targeting voting infrastructure ahead of the midterm elections.[130][131][132]

Pro-Trump television ads

Five weeks before the midterm elections, the Department of Homeland Security allocated $20M in taxpayer funds initially reserved for Customs and Border Protection from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to air campaign-style television ads promoting Donald Trump, drawing widespread bipartisan criticism.[133] The White House defended the ads as "public service announcements" aimed at promoting patriotism rather than campaigning. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters, "I like the message, but it shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer money."[134] Multiple legal experts contacted by the Associated Press said the advertisements likely violated federal law prohibiting "publicity or propaganda".[135] Following widespread criticism, Trump announced he would pay for the ads via a campaign account, but did not commit to reimbursing the government the $12M already spent on the ad campaign.[136] On October 11, a federal judge issued an order to stop the airing of Trump administration television advertisements funded by taxpayer money, but two other advertisements were also broadcast after the deadline set by the court. The next day, Justice Department lawyers apologized for the incident, saying that legal counsel had not been informed of the court's order in time.[137]

Overall, advertising spending for the 2026 midterm elections surpassed $10 billion by the middle of October.[138]

Political donations

Since July, Elon Musk has spent more than $276 million on right-wing political groups to help maintain the Republican majority. With total spending of about $366 million, he has become the largest donor in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.[139] The donations include $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the largest supporter of Republican Senate candidates, $76 million to America PAC, and $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, which supports Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate in Texas, running against Democratic candidate James Talarico.[140]

As the 2026 election enters its final stages, spending by super PACs and dark money is reaching record levels. Hundreds of millions of dollars have been paid by major donors to influence government policy, And the largest donors also tend to lean more toward the Republican Party. Public anger over the role of money in politics is growing, and both parties have promised to fight corruption if they win. By law, super PACs must operate independently of candidates, but in practice, candidates and these groups often work in close coordination. For example, Trump has repeatedly referred to funds raised by the super PAC "MAGA Inc." as his own money, and he has control over it.

Election prediction markets

During the 2026 US midterm elections, betting on election outcomes on prediction platforms such as Polymarket and Kalshi has increased significantly. According to a Reuters report on October 14, 2026, an analysis by the Anti-Corruption Data Collective (ACDC) shows that trading volume in these platforms' election markets has exceeded $220 million, while the figure was about $92 million in the 2024 congressional elections.[141]

Kalshi and Polymarket have partnered with various news organisations for election coverage. For instance, in December 2025, Kalshi partnered with CNN in order to include their data in news coverage. A similar deal was struck between Polymarket and Yahoo finance.[142]

Alaska Senate election legal proceedings

On October 23, 2026, President Trump announced he had personally requested the Department of Justice to file a lawsuit arguing that the 2026 Senate election in Alaska should not be certified if Democrat Mary Peltola wins.[143] The justification in the filing is based on two similarly named Republican candidates, incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., appearing on the ballot may lead to voter confusion.[144] J. Sullivan Jr. was previously affirmed by the state's Supreme Court to appear on the ballot when state election officials made allegations that his candidacy was an intended spoiler.[145] The federal suit was dismissed by U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason on November 1.[146]

On October 28, Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy announced a state criminal investigation into Peltola's campaign after the New York Times reported staffers may have intentionally recruited candidates such as J. Sullivan Jr. to be spoilers.[147] On October 30 it was revealed that a federal investigation has been underway "for several months" already.[148]

Louisiana v. Callais

Further information: Louisiana v. Callais
These paragraphs are an excerpt from Louisiana v. Callais § Analysis.[edit]

Analysts had predicted that a decision in Callais reducing the scope of the VRA could allow Republicans to gain a significant number of seats in the U.S. House of Representatives from redistricting in the Southeast, where the VRA has generally prevented Republican-controlled legislatures from maximizing their numbers of "safe" districts. The New York Times estimated that, if the Court weakened the VRA, up to twelve seats could shift from Democratic to Republican control.[149][150]

When the decision in Callais was announced, media outlets characterized it as a "landmark" decision, predicting that the additional restrictions on Section 2 of the VRA would likely make challenges to redistricting significantly more difficult. Analysts expect it will allow southern states to eliminate majority-minority districts, changing election outcomes.[151][152][153][154] The decision was seen by lawyers as the culmination of a long-time grudge of Roberts against the VRA,[155][156][157] while media outlets considered the decision as rendering the VRA all but dead and harming the country's democratic process.[158][159] The ruling was described by critics as starting a new era of Jim Crow laws, allowing for legal discrimination of minorities in the United States.[160][161] The court's opinion was expected to affect all levels of government including state and local governments.[162][163][164][165]

An analysis from The Guardian found that Justice Alito's claim that Black voter turnout had surpassed white voter turnout in two of the five most recent presidential elections, both nationally and in Louisiana, was based on misleading data and questionable methodology. Alito cited the brief from the Department of Justice which used "a proportion of the total population of each racial group over the age of 18"; however, that approach is "not favored by experts", who instead use "voter turnout as a proportion of the citizen voting age population or the voter eligible population." Following the latter analysis, the gap in voter turnout has actually widened, with Black voter turnout dropping since 2012, particularly after the Supreme Court's opinion in Shelby County v. Holder which struck down the preclearance formula defined in Section 4(b) of the VRA for states with historical discrimination concerns including Louisiana.[166][167]

White House media ban

This section is an excerpt from Donald Trump's conflict with the news media.[edit]

Donald Trump frequently attacks the American media as having a left-wing bias and being "corrupt", and also uses a variety of insults when speaking about outlets that give him unfavorable coverage. Trump has sued various media outlets for perceived inaccuracies or biases, and has used his position as president to pressure outlets he dislikes by interfering in their business operations, launching investigations, threatening to revoke broadcast licenses, and cutting funding for public broadcasting.

In September 2026, Trump barred CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House grounds. The three outlets filed suit, arguing that the ban violated due process and First Amendment protections. The move drew criticism from Republican strategists, who warned that it diverted attention from economic issues ahead of the midterms.[168]

Issues

The lead-up to the elections was marked by an inflation surge amidst the United States affordability crisis, including on gas, healthcare, and food prices, with the executive branch raising federal revenue by imposing the largest tax hikes in American history through tariffs. Other shared concerns cited by voters include a perception of corruption and self-dealing; democratic backsliding; mass surveillance; and foreign policy, including declining relations with American allies, a proposed rapprochement with Russia, coerced expansionism, and an escalating rift with the Vatican. The Trump administration politically aligned with Silicon Valley and encouraged the development of artificial superintelligence through the construction of AI data centers, and there has been a public backlash to the potential prospect of widespread job loss through AGI, its environmental impacts, and the existential risk it poses. The administration campaigned on changing the English language to be in line with the president, including Lake Ontario ("Lake America") and Gulf of Mexico ("Gulf of America"), while Democrats labeled the changes a distraction from important issues.

Cost of living

The economy, including gas prices, inflation, healthcare, tariffs, and cost of living, is one of the primary issues of the election.[169] The second Trump administration imposed the largest tax increase in American history in April 2025, with an expected six trillion dollars in returned taxation if maintained until 2035, on much of the world with the intent to re-industrialize the United States.[170] It was criticized by experts and global leaders for worsening inflation.[171][172][173][174]

Fuel costs were increased by the 2026 Iran war.[175] The Trump administration announced in October 2026 that it would buy diesel from Russia and suspend sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027. The move was intended to lower fuel prices before the November elections.[176] A group of seven senators — four Republicans and three Democrats — criticized the decision. They said it violates the 2022 congressional ban on Russian energy imports. They also said the administration neither consulted Congress nor gave the required legal justification. At the same time, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the agreement, saying the government was acting under existing legal authority and that the deal would reduce prices.[177] Trade, including tariffs, has been a leading issue of the campaign season.[178]

Data released on October 14, 2026, by the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed US annual inflation rising to 3.7 per cent in September. That marked an increase from 3.4 per cent in August and exceeded the 3.6 per cent forecast by economists in a Bloomberg poll. It was the first uptick since May. Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, also surpassed Wall Street expectations, climbing to 2.6 per cent from 2.4 per cent the month before.[179]

In the final weeks before the elections, the Trump administration pledged to provide U.S. farmers and ranchers with an agricultural aid and bailout package worth more than $15 billion. The programs, which include an $8 billion Harvest Fuel Relief Program to offset high diesel and operating costs, were criticized by political analysts who describe the timing as targeted electoral outreach while also receiving support for stabilizing rural economies.[180]

Corruption

Main article: Corruption allegations during the second Trump presidency

According to a September 2026 Gallup poll, 89% of people believe that there is pervasive corruption within the US government.[181] While in office, Trump has engaged in unprecedented self-enrichment and faced widespread allegations of corruption.[182][183] Trump's grants of pardons and clemency have favored political allies and loyalists, with several given after millions in donations or fees.[184]

January 17, 2025[185]

Trump has proactively solicited donations from companies and individuals following which favorable regulatory actions and decisions have occurred. He has maintained an active stock market account with thousands of trades totaling hundreds of millions of dollars.[186] Trump has directly benefited by soliciting his own memecoin, $TRUMP and from his family's cryptocurrency company World Liberty Financial which has received investments by anonymous individuals and foreign governments.[187]

According to analysis from The New York Times, anonymous political contributions to the midterm elections, known as "dark money," exceeded $1 billion by late August. This funding is funneled into Super PACs through nonprofit organizations and shell companies, allowing donors to remain undisclosed.[175]

Democracy

The United States has suffered from political dysfunction and immense erosion in democratic health.[188] Polling has indicated that voters are afraid of the nation becoming authoritarian.[189] The large majority of Americans favor radical changes to the nation's political system, including abolishing the electoral college and replacing it with a direct popular vote, implementing campaign spending limits, and enacting age limits for the Supreme Court of the United States.[190]

The Senate has also become a subject for reform, and is one of the "most unloved institutions"[191] in the country, seen as systematically designed to favor the interests of an American oligarchy.[192]

Artificial intelligence

AI became a leading concern for voters.[193] Opposition to water, energy, and pollution-intensive data centers, and artificial intelligence more broadly,[194] emerged as an unexpected issue during the election.[195][196][197][198][199] The Brookings Institution described the backlash as part of a broader opposition against "AI power".[200] Republicans in the election generally took stances in the midterm more favorable to Silicon Valley, the construction of data centers, and the future of AI development than Democratic candidates, although the issue was not as partisanized as others.[201][202]

Concerns included widespread unemployment through artificial general intelligence's development,[203] imposition of mass surveillance,[204] and the existential risk of superintelligence to humanity.[205][206][204][207] A bipartisan group in Congress of conservatives, liberals, socialists, and populists has united in opposition to transhumanist and post-humanist ideals in AI development, including Republican senator Josh Hawley, right-wing populist Steve Bannon, Democratic representative Greg Casar, and independent senator Bernie Sanders.[208]

On September 29, 2026, President Trump signed an executive order to replace the term "Artificial Intelligence" (AI) with "Super Intelligence" (SI) in official communications and documents. The order mandates all government agencies to use this terminology, including technologies that do not fit the accepted definition of superintelligence.[209]

Data centers

A September 2026 poll found that 70% of Americans oppose data center construction in their own communities. AI opposition has occurred across bipartisan lines, described as "sweeping the globe" by Politico.[205] A September 2026 Quinnipac University poll found that 73% of Americans "would oppose the building of an AI data center in their community" while 21% would support it.[206]

Mass surveillance

The Trump administration has implemented mass surveillance in the United States through the development of artificial intelligence technologies.[210][211][212] Flock cameras and other video surveillance have been rapidly constructed on American streets since the beginning of his term, with Trump saying that "I like them" in September 2026.[213] There have been arguments made that the U.S. is taking on the characteristics of a surveillance state.[214]

Democrats have called for stricter privacy laws modeled on the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation. Republicans have generally believed that mass survelliance improves safety, and that individuals should be willing to give up aspects of privacy in return for protection.[215]

Renaming of English terminology

President Trump and the Republican Party campaigned on changing English terminology for emerging technologies and geographic landmarks, including the Gulf of Mexico, New Mexico, artificial intelligence, and the Atlantic Ocean.[216] In May 2025, Republicans passed a bill in the House of Representatives to rename the "Gulf of Mexico" into the "Gulf of America".[217] The Trump administration and Republicans have used it to portray Democrats as unpatriotic.[218]

Foreign policy

Expansionism

These paragraphs are an excerpt from American expansionism under Donald Trump.[edit]

Throughout both of his presidencies, U.S. president Donald Trump has expressed a desire to expand the United States' territory and influence through both land purchases and military means.

Trump first stated his desire to annex Greenland during his first presidency; he has pursued a campaign to acquire Greenland during his second presidency. He has also suggested annexation or taking control of Canada, Iceland, Mexico, Cuba, the Panama Canal and Gaza Strip. After proposing an invasion of Venezuela during his first presidency, Trump's second administration removed President Nicolás Maduro as part of Operation Absolute Resolve and stated the U.S. would "run" Venezuela; the Venezuelan government, led by acting president Delcy Rodríguez, remains in place but is far more amicable to American interests than it was under Maduro.[224] Threats were also made against Colombia and then-president Gustavo Petro, which Trump accused of drug trafficking.[225] Amid the 2026 Iran war, Trump lauded about invading and seizing control of both the Strait of Hormuz and Kharg Island from Iran.

Trump's determination to treat the Western Hemisphere as a U.S. sphere of influence has been characterized as a revival of the Monroe Doctrine in what has become known as the Donroe Doctrine. On his orders, U.S. federal agencies adopted new names for shared international waters, renaming the Gulf of Mexico as "Gulf of America" in 2025 and Lake Ontario as "Lake America" in 2026. Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the second Trump administration's foreign policy as a matter of operating as a superpower nation and for national security purposes. Numerous politicians outside the U.S. have criticized Trump's annexation comments. The Democratic Party has introduced bills to prevent the Trump administration from invading countries without the approval of Congress.

2026 Iran war

A main topics during the election campaign trail was the joint conflict with Iran with Israel.[226]

The war was preceded by the largest US military buildup in the region since the 2003 invasion of Iraq.[227] It resulted in thousands of civilian and military casualties. The economic impact of the war included the largest supply disruption of the global oil market, disruptions of the natural gas, fertilizer, aviation, and tourism industries, and financial volatility.[227] As of October 2026[update], the US Department of Defense estimated that the war had so far cost $47.1 billion.[228]

American rationale for initiating the war included regime change, preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, a response to the massacre of anti-government protesters in Iran, and seizing Iran's resources.[227] Critics have rejected these justifications, stating that the attack is a war of aggression and illegal.[227] Initially setting upon a course to overthrow the Iranian government, later goals focused on nuclear negotiations and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.[227]

Public opinion was opposed to the war in the U.S. and in many other countries, leading to disapproval for Donald Trump and declining views of the US and Israel around the world.[227] Also, according to two polls conducted by Fox News and the Associated Press-NORC between October 8 and 12, 2026, the Iran war has become one of the most important concerns for voters in the midterm elections, surpassing immigration and crime. A Fox News poll showed that 60% of voters oppose US military action against Iran and prefer Democratic congressional candidates.[229]

Democrats also criticized the administration's handling of the war, including Hegseth's role as defense secretary. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said that Democrats would seek Hegseth's removal if they gained control of the House in the midterm elections. According to The Atlantic, Democrats were also considering investigations and possible impeachment proceedings, as well as other measures such as hearings, subpoenas, and restrictions on defense spending.[230]

According to an October 2026 report by the Financial Times, Donald Trump blocked an Israeli plan for a multi-day military operation against Iran that had been scheduled for the weekend of 10 October. The report stated that Trump did not want a new military conflict to begin just before the 3 November midterm elections.[231] A Middle East Monitor analysis interpreted the decision as an effort by both leaders to protect their own electoral positions: Trump sought to preserve Republican seats, while Benjamin Netanyahu's deferral of the operation was seen as a way to protect Likud's hold on power.[232][233]

The advocacy organization Republicans Overseas Israel estimates that approximately 500,000 Israelis holding American passports are eligible to vote in both US and Israeli elections. Marc Zell, the group's chairman, believes these voters could significantly affect tight US races, such as the Senate race in Michigan. Their collaborative military efforts against Iran further strengthen the bond between the two nations. While a Democratic majority in Congress might reduce US backing for Israel, President Trump retains significant executive authority.[234]

The Iranian government was accused by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on 20 October, of using World War II era U-boat tactics. Rubio stated that this was the first time a nation-state had openly targeted civilian sailors and commercial vessels since 1945.[235][236] Rubio reaffirmed Washington's commitment to applying "extraordinary economic pressure" to prevent Tehran from funding regional proxies.[237]

On 29 October, British newspaper The Daily Telegraph reported that the Iranian regime is aiming to disrupt the elections after attempting to meddle with the 2026 Israeli legislative election this week.[238]

On 30 October, Trump stated that he believes the war will finish soon and that the US requires a guaranty that Iran would never possess a nuclear weapon.[239]

Religious conflicts, rift with the Holy See

Since Pope Leo XIV's election as Pope in 2025,[240] the Trump administration has made direct attacks on the Pope, the Catholic Church, and the Holy See that were described by scholars as historically unparalleled by any Western government in the modern era.[241][242] The issue saw widespread attention during the election, and Mainline Protestants, Catholics, and evangelical Protestants shifted by double-digits in polling towards Independent and Democratic candidates, alleging that Trump's policies, behavior, and political agenda were in direct contradiction to the tenets of Christian morality.[243] Over 30 pastors ran as Democrats in the 2026 election,[244] and Reuters said that many of its candidates ran on socially conservative or moderate positions.[245]

After genocidal threats were made by Donald Trump to Iran on April 7 saying "a whole civilization will die", Pope Leo XIV called for peace.[246] On April 12, 2026, President Donald Trump directly criticized the pope in a Truth Social post, writing that "Pope Leo is WEAK on Crime, and terrible for Foreign Policy," and "catering to the Radical Left".[241] Marco Politi, a long time Vatican observer and author, stated: "You have to jump back to the Middle Ages when kings and emperors were shouting against the pope in Rome and calling him false. There is just no other recent example like this."[242] Academic Andrew Chestnut stated, "I cannot think of any parallels, at least coming from Western Christian majority countries, of such pointed and public attacks on the Pope."[247]

Another dispute between the Holy See and the Trump administration emerged in the last two weeks of the midterm election,[243] after "12 clergymen joined Trump on Thursday in the Oval Office", for what Archbishop Jeffrey Grob of Milwaukee has said was intended to be a private meeting to discuss matters such as "immigration enforcement, religious worker visas, and human dignity" but was falsely portrayed by the administration as a midterm religious endorsement.[243] Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines said that the meeting had been "exploited" and that "there are many things tied to this present [Trump] Administration that are blatantly at odds with our Catholic faith."[243] Pope Leo XIV voted by mail in the midterm election, becoming the first pontiff to vote in a secular election.[248]

Federal elections

Senate elections

Main article: 2026 United States Senate elections
2026 United States elections

35 seats in the United States Senate will be up for election, including all 33 Class 2 seats. Republicans gained majority control of the Senate in the 2024 elections by flipping four Democratic seats. Two Democratic-held seats, Georgia and Michigan, are in states won by Donald Trump in the previous presidential election, while Maine is the only Republican-held seat in a state won by Kamala Harris.

Special elections

Two special elections will be held to fill the unexpired terms of senators who vacated their seats during the 119th Congress:

  • Florida Class 3: Republican Marco Rubio resigned his seat on January 20, 2025, to become U.S. secretary of state under the second Trump administration. Ashley Moody was appointed by Florida governor Ron DeSantis to fill the seat until the special election, which will take place concurrently with the regularly scheduled 2026 elections.[249]
  • Ohio Class 3: Republican JD Vance resigned his seat on January 10, 2025, following his election as vice president of the United States. Jon Husted was appointed by Ohio governor Mike DeWine to fill the seat until the special election, which will take place concurrently with the regularly scheduled 2026 elections.[250]

House of Representatives elections

Main article: 2026 United States House of Representatives elections
See also: 2025–2026 United States redistricting

All 435 voting seats in the United States House of Representatives will be up for election. Additionally, elections will be held to select the non-voting delegate for the District of Columbia and the non-voting delegates from 4 of the 5 U.S. territories, excluding Puerto Rico due to its non-voting delegate serving a 4-year term. There are 16 Democratic incumbents in districts Donald Trump won, while only 8 Republican incumbents are in seats won by Harris.[251]

The House map features a number of new congressional maps: Ohio and Utah will have new, court-mandated congressional districts this cycle; Missouri, North Carolina, and Texas redrew their maps mid-cycle; and the district map was changed in California following the passage of Prop 50.[252][253][254][255][256]

In Missouri, the legality of a Republican-backed congressional map remained disputed in September 2026. On September 8, Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh declined to intervene in an emergency appeal seeking to allow the new map to be used in the November election. Hours later, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark issued a temporary order requiring Missouri to use the Republican-backed map, conflicting with Missouri Supreme Court ruling that had blocked its use and ordered a referendum on the map. The competing rulings left the state's congressional districts unresolved ahead of the general election.[257] However, on September 10, the U.S. Supreme Court stayed Judge Clark's order whilst a federal lawsuit filed by Republican nominees Bob Onder and Rick Brattin for the 3rd and 5th districts respectively, played out.[258] The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit then fast-tracked the case for a hearing on September 17 and, ruling on the merits, affirmed the lower courts order on September 21, remanding the case back to the District Court for entry of a permanent injunction but stayed their ruling for a week pending an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.[259][260] On September 25, the U.S. Supreme Court unanimously held that state law rules in the case and granted an emergency stay of the Eighth Circuit's order and Judge Clark's injunction, leaving the 2022 maps in place for the 2026 elections. The court also faulted the District Court and the Eighth Circuit for what it deemed as having "incorrectly applied" the Purcell Principle and further held that the Supreme Court of Missouri was not at fault for "upsetting the status quo".[261]

Special elections

Six special elections to the House of Representatives were held in 2026.

  • Texas's 18th congressional district: Democrat Christian Menefee defeated fellow Democrat Amanda Edwards in a runoff to succeed Democrat Sylvester Turner, who died on March 5, 2025.[262][263] The district has a partisan index of D+21.[264]
  • Georgia's 14th congressional district: Republican Clay Fuller defeated Democrat Shawn Harris in a runoff to succeed Republican Marjorie Taylor Greene, who resigned on January 5, 2026.[265] The district has a partisan index of R+19.[264]
  • New Jersey's 11th congressional district: Democrat Analilia Mejia defeated Republican Joe Hathaway to succeed Democrat Mikie Sherrill, who resigned on November 20, 2025, to take office as governor of New Jersey.[266] The district has a partisan index of D+5.[264]
  • California's 1st congressional district: Republican James Gallagher defeated Democrats Audrey Denney and Mike McGuire to succeed Republican Doug LaMalfa, who died on January 6, 2026.[267] The district has a partisan index of R+12.[264]
  • California's 14th congressional district: Democrat Aisha Wahab defeated fellow Democrat Melissa Hernandez in a runoff to succeed Democrat Eric Swalwell, who resigned on April 14, 2026, following accusations of sexual misconduct.[268] The district has a partisan index of D+20.[264]
  • Georgia's 13th congressional district: Democrat Everton Blair defeated fellow Democrat Marcye Scott in a runoff to succeed Democrat David Scott, who died on April 22, 2026.[269] This district has a partisan index of D+21.[264]

State elections

Gubernatorial elections

See also: 2026 United States gubernatorial elections

36 states and three territories will be holding regularly scheduled gubernatorial elections. The governors of 15 states and two territories are term-limited. Prior to the 2026 gubernatorial elections, Republicans control 26 of the 50 state governorships, and each party holds 18 state governorships up for election.[275] Republicans have held a majority of the state governorships since the 2010 elections.[276]

Lieutenant gubernatorial elections

See also: 2026 United States lieutenant gubernatorial elections

Nine states will be holding lieutenant gubernatorial elections independently from their gubernatorial elections.

Attorney general elections

See also: 2026 United States attorney general elections

30 states, two territories, and one federal district will be holding regularly scheduled attorney general elections.

Secretary of state elections

See also: 2026 United States secretary of state elections

26 states will be holding regularly scheduled secretary of state elections.

Treasurer elections

See also: 2026 United States state treasurer elections

27 states will be holding regularly scheduled treasurer elections.

Auditor elections

Main article: 2026 United States state auditor elections

23 states will be holding regularly scheduled auditor elections.

Legislative elections

See also: 2026 United States state legislative elections

88 state legislative chambers and 5 territorial chambers will be holding regularly scheduled elections. Republicans have held a majority of the state legislative chambers and seats since the 2010 elections. Prior to the regularly-scheduled 2026 state legislative elections, Republicans hold 4044 state legislative seats, while Democrats hold 3227 state legislative seats.[276]

State judicial elections

Main article: 2026 United States judicial elections

Elections are scheduled to be held in 2026, in various states across the country, including supreme courts and appellate courts.

Ballot measures

See also: 2026 United States ballot measures

100 ballot measures in 37 states will be held in the November election.[277]

Local elections

Main article: 2026 United States local elections

Local elections will be held in the United States throughout 2026 to elect officers of municipal and county governments. At least 22 mayorships in the country's top 100 most populous cities will be up for election, and many more will hold elections for local ballot measures, city council, and numerous other municipal offices. Many of these races will coincide with the 2026 midterm elections.

Municipal mayoral elections

A number of major cities will hold mayoral elections in 2026.

Incumbents re-elected

  • Arlington, Texas: Two-term incumbent Jim Ross was re-elected for a third term.[278] Independent hold
  • Auburn, Alabama: Two-term incumbent Ron Anders Jr. was re-elected for a third term.[279] Independent hold

  • Union City, New Jersey: Seven-term incumbent Democrat Brian P. Stack was re-elected for an eighth term.[290] Democratic hold

Incumbents defeated

  • Ann Arbor, Michigan: Three-term incumbent Christopher Taylor lost renomination in the Democratic primary to Yousef Rabhi.[291]
  • Pierre, South Dakota: Three-term incumbent Steve Harding was defeated for re-election by Todd Johnson.[292]
  • Providence, Rhode Island: One-term incumbent Brett Smiley lost renomination in the Democratic primary to David Morales.[293]
  • Richmond, California: One-term incumbent Democrat Eduardo Martinez lost renomination to fellow Democrats Ahmad Anderson and Claudia Jimenez.[294]
  • River Falls, Wisconsin: One-term incumbent Republican Dan Toland was defeated for re-election by Democrat Alison Page.[295] Democratic gain
  • Salem, Oregon: One-term incumbent Independent Julie Hoy was defeated for re-election by Democrat Vanessa Nordyke.[296] Democratic gain

Open seats won

  • Boca Raton, Florida: Three-term incumbent Republican Scott Singer was ineligible for re-election due to term limits. Democrat Andy Thomson defeated Republicans Fran Nachlas and Mike Liebelson.[297] Democratic gain
  • Cataño, Puerto Rico (special): Incumbent Julio Alicea Vassallo died of cancer. New Progressive Hiram Torres Montalvo defeated fellow New Progressive Bethzaida Rodríguez Torres. New Progressive hold[298]
  • Chandler, Arizona: Two-term incumbent Kevin Hartke was term-limited and ineligible to run. Democrat Matt Orlando defeated Republican Jeff Weninger.[299] Democratic gain
  • Fargo, North Dakota: Two-term incumbent Tim Mahoney was term-limited and ineligible to run. Democrat Josh Boschee was elected.[300] Democratic hold
  • Independence, Missouri: One-term incumbent Rory Rowland decided not to run for re-election. Kevin King defeated Bridget McCandless.[301]
  • Irving, Texas: Three-term incumbent Rick Stopfer was term-limited and ineligible to run. Republican Albert C. Zapanta defeated Zhanae Jackson and Olivia Novelo Abreu. Republican hold
  • Leander, Texas: Incumbent Republican Christine DeLisle resigned 1 year and 5 months into her second term. Democrat Na'Cole Thompson defeated Mike Sanders and Kathryn Pantalion-Parker.[302] Democratic gain
  • Montpelier, Vermont: Two-term incumbent Democrat John McCullough retired. Marc Gwinn won unopposed.[303]
  • Pearland, Texas: One-term incumbent Republican Kevin Cole decided not to run for re-election. Democrat Quentin Wiltz defeated Republican Tony Carbone.[304] Democratic gain
  • Sioux Falls, South Dakota: Two-term incumbent Paul TenHaken was term-limited and ineligible to run. Republican Christine Erickson defeated Democrat Jamie Smith.[305] Republican hold
  • Waukesha, Wisconsin: Three-term incumbent Independent Shawn Reilly decided not to run for re-election. Democrat Alicia Halvensleben defeated Republican Scott Allen.[306] Democratic gain

Table of state, territorial, and federal results

See also: Political party strength in U.S. states

This table shows the partisan results of congressional, gubernatorial, and state legislative races held in each state and territory in 2026. Note that not all states and territories hold gubernatorial, state legislative, and Senate elections in 2026, and some seats in the U.S. House of Representatives will be vacant at the time of the regularly-scheduled 2026 elections. The five territories and Washington, D.C. do not elect members of the Senate; instead, they each elect one non-voting member of the House. Nebraska's unicameral legislature and the governorship and the legislature of American Samoa are elected on a non-partisan basis, and political party affiliation is not listed.

Debates

The 2026 elections had a record number of elections that did not have any formal debates. 21 out of 36 races for governors did not have a debate. In the 2018 midterm elections, only two of the 36 had no debates. Of the 35 Senate seats up for election, 21 didn't have any debates.[844]
